chunks: "The half-bridge is one leg: two FETs and a single output node.
It can drive a load between that node and a fixed rail, so a motor on a half-bridge only sees zero to the supply voltage and only spins one way.
It's cheaper, has one FET in the current path, and it's all you need for a fan, a heater, a solenoid or a buck converter.
The H-bridge is two legs, four FETs, and the motor floats between the two outputs.
That gives me plus or minus the full supply from a single rail, so I get both directions, active braking and regeneration back to the supply.
The price is twice the parts, twice the gate drivers, two FETs in series in the current path so double the conduction loss, and more ways to shoot through.

You can get a bipolar output from a half-bridge by returning the load to a mid-point made of two capacitors, but then the load only sees half the supply and the capacitors carry the full load current, so it's not free.
My rule: unidirectional load, use a half-bridge; need reverse or full-voltage bipolar drive, use an H-bridge; three-phase motor, three half-bridges."
